articles.subtitle: James Turner Pokémon As one of Kotaku ’s resident Pokémon guys, I’ve seen quotes from developers at Game Freak and creatives at The Pokémon Company floating around for decades.
articles.author: Kotaku
articles.content:
James Turner Pokémon

As one of Kotaku ’s resident Pokémon guys, I’ve seen quotes from developers at Game Freak and creatives at The Pokémon Company floating around for decades. Today I’m thinking back on one from James Turner, the newly crowned Creative Director of Pokémon Art and Design at TPC, having returned to the Pokémon world after leaving Game Freak in 2022.

Turner’s return is either exciting or controversial, depending on how you feel about the various Pokémon and other characters he designed during his many years at Game Freak.

But regardless of whether you have a crush on Scarlet and Violet ’s hot professors or you harbor a strong dislike for the infamous ice cream Pokémon Vanillite, most Pokémon fans know that Turner knows (Poké) ball, and I want to highlight how he spoke about designing these critters in a 2019 interview.

Big news! I’ve started a new role as Creative Director of Pokémon Art and Design at The Pokémon Company International. It feels great to be working in the world of Pokémon again, with a lovely group of people. I’m very excited about what comes next! 🎨⚡ #IWorkForPokemon pic.twitter.com/HHugqAxpZv — James Turner (@JamesTurner_42) August 24, 2026

Big news! I’ve started a new role as Creative Director of Pokémon Art and Design at The Pokémon Company International.

It feels great to be working in the world of Pokémon again, with a lovely group of people.

I’m very excited about what comes next! 🎨⚡ #IWorkForPokemon pic.twitter.com/HHugqAxpZv

— James Turner (@JamesTurner_42) August 24, 2026

Back in 2019, Game Informer was doing a cover story on Pokémon Sword and Shield, and while the Switch RPGs were a touchy subject for some fans at the time because this was when Game Freak stopped allowing players to catch and transfer every Pokémon in one game, we’re now distanced enough from them that a lot of folks look back on them more fondly.

Turner was the art director on Sword and Shield, and designed a handful of the Pokémon that players met in the Galar region, as well as alternate forms of old favorites like the big Gigantamax Pikachu that harkens back to the electric mouse’s rounder days in the early years of the series.

In the interview, Turner talks about the design philosophy of creating Pokémon, and how artists have different, distinct styles that they have to, in some way, apply to the same universe’s rules and vibe. How do you make Pokémon like a cute little Pikachu and an intimidating literal god like Arceus look so different and yet still be part of the same universe?

Turner’s explanation is one of my favorite summations of what makes Pokémon a universal experience, whether you like the cute, cool, terrifying, or weird little guys.

“I would say that an important thing is that every Pokémon you feel like you could be friends with,” Turner says. “They can’t just be intimidating, they can’t just be scary, there has to be something there that makes you think, ‘Oh, I could be friends with this Pokémon. They could be on my team, we could go into an adventure together.’”

The example he gives of a Pokémon that might be intimidating at first blush is Buzzwole, one of the Ultra Beasts from Generation VI that is quite literally meant to look otherworldly and almost un-Pokémon-like. It’s a bug/fighting-type monster that looks like a cross between a buff superhero and a mosquito, but according to Turner, that “silliness” makes something that could be terrifying look like something you could reasonably catch and pal around with.

Speaking as someone whose team of favorites includes the literal god of space, I feel like Pokémon has done a good job of making even the series’ monstrosities feel like something you can imagine your character having a connection with, and that plays a big part in the “every Pokémon is someone’s favorite” talking point.

There are over 1000 of these creatures now, and even if there are some you think are ugly or annoying, there’s probably something that draws another fan to them, and I feel like Turner’s philosophy here illustrates why.

Turner’s created a lot of Pokémon and human characters over the years, and even if you don’t love every one he’s made, I do think having him back at the company is going to be a net positive. The guy just gets it, and he designed my Pokémon daddy Professor Turo, so he can do whatever he wants.

Plug your MacBook in and out of a multi-port laptop docking station to swiftly add multiple devices and external displays with just one cable connection to your laptop. We tested the top contenders to find the best Thunderbolt and USB-C docks available to owners of the MacBook Air and MacBook Pro. MacBook Neo users can use any of these docks but are limited to a 10Gbps bandwidth and some display limitations.

Thunderbolt, USB4 or USB-C

The connectors all look the same (technically known as a “Type-C connector”), but there are significant differences, particularly on speed that will determine both data-transfer rate and higher external display refresh rates.

USB-C: 5Gbps or 10Gbps

USB4: 20Gbps or 40Gbps

Thunderbolt 3 and 4: 40Gbps

Thunderbolt 5: 80Gbps / 120Gbps

Our list Which ports does my MacBook have will show you how many USB-C or more likely one of Thunderbolt 3, 4 or 5 that you have.

While a Thunderbolt 4 (TB4) dock will be enough for most casual users, if you can stretch the budget go for a TB5 dock as it will remain current for years, saving you money in the long term, and is backwards compatible with earlier versions and all the way back to USB-C. High-end professionals should always aim for Thunderbolt 5.

The dock needs one (“ upstream “) Thunderbolt or USB-C port for connecting to and charging your laptop (although all recent MacBooks can also power via the MagSafe 3 port), and at least another (“ downstream “) to attach further devices (hard drives, external display, and others).

The USB-C MacBook Neo has just the one data port, with the other reserved for charging. A dock with Power Delivery will greatly expand the entry-level Mac laptop.

For more detail, read our Thunderbolt 5 vs Thunderbolt 4 vs Thunderbolt 3 vs USB4 explainer.

Add external displays to your MacBook

If you use your laptop as your principal computer, attaching at least one larger display to create a hybrid desktop/laptop setup, with a keyboard and mouse, will boost your productivity. You can turn that 13in MacBook’s cramped screen real-estate into an iconic iMac-sized 27in or even larger screen by adding an extra display—or connect two or even four large monitors to extend your screen across your whole desk.

Take a look at our recommended best monitors and displays for Mac and also the best portable monitors for Mac.

You’ll get two or more Extended mode screens (where the screen extends beyond what you can see on the laptop screen) using a Thunderbolt connection (or DisplayPort/HDMI).

Natively over mere USB-C, Macs can connect to only one external display in Extended mode, as opposed to Mirrored mode (which replicates exactly what you get on the laptop screen) but DisplayLink is third-party software that allows some docks to extend to up to four screens on even the most basic Mac.

DisplayLink-supporting docks are also the only way that non-Pro/Max M1 and M2 MacBooks can connect more than one external display.

articles.title: Big Walk: A Good Hang with Friends
articles.subtitle: I dove into Big Walk with no expectations at all. I’d seen trailers leading up to the launch and knew that it was a co-op puzzle game from House House, the makers of Untitled Goose Game, but that was about it.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
I dove into Big Walk with no expectations at all. I’d seen trailers leading up to the launch and knew that it was a co-op puzzle game from House House, the makers of Untitled Goose Game, but that was about it. And because most of my gaming is done solo, I initially tuned out most of the game’s post-launch headlines. Still, Big Walk is published by Panic, which has a great track record for finding and publishing great indie games, so I decided to give it a try earlier this week. And you know what? I love it.

Big Walk is about as low-key as a puzzle game gets in the best possible way. Co-op is the only mode, so you’ll need to coordinate a time to play it with a friend or group. One person takes the lead, setting up the session and inviting the others. The process is far simpler than trying to find a time that works for everyone in your group.

As players join, you’re dropped into a space to wait for the others and explore a little. This lobby space is where you’ll learn the game’s controls, too. Big Walk supports keyboard and mouse input as well as a controller, which is what I used, playing on an M4 Max MacBook Pro.

Once you get your bearings, it’s time to exit the lobby and start exploring. That exploration is core to what Big Walk is all about. You aren’t told what to do, but there are just enough clues to push you forward, figuring out the goals on your own without too much trouble.

I played using AirPods Pro 3, and the game made great use of their mics and speakers, simulating the environments we were in. Closed spaces were echoey, and speech was distant and faint when we were separated. Sound even becomes part of the mechanic in some puzzles, such as an early one where you have to look through an open window to hear each other properly and help guide the other player’s actions.

That cooperation is the key part of the game’s loop. You may see how to solve Big Walk’s puzzles on your own, but implementing the solution will require you and a companion to work together.

The togetherness of it all extends beyond the puzzles, too. Big Walk’s environment (at least in the early stages) is mountainous with large rocks and trees that make it possible to get separated from others. Add to that day and night cycles where it’s almost impossible to see where you’re going at night without a light, and you have every incentive not to wander off on your own without a plan for how to reconnect.

I’ve played through Big Walk’s first couple of sections, and it was a blast. The puzzles were clever and challenging without being frustrating, but most of all, I enjoyed working through them with someone else. There’s no time pressure or monsters lurking around corners – just puzzles and a chance to chat.

Ultimately, that’s what makes Big Walk work. It’s a good hang built against the backdrop of a beautiful landscape and low-key, fun challenges. I highly recommend giving it a try.

Big Walk, which supports crossplay and 2–12 players, is available on the Mac App Store for $14.99. The game is also on Steam, the Switch 2, and PS5.

articles.title: Microsoft had to change the anti-piracy hologram on the Windows 95 box because an undisclosed government assumed the baby on it was naked
articles.subtitle: Microsoft says the government "shall remain nameless for obvious reasons".
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
Did you know there are two different holograms on old boxes of Windows 95? I didn't. Did you know one of them has a child with no top pointing at Microsoft on a monitor, which a government complained about and got changed? I also did not know that.

Yet now I do, thanks to a blog from Microsoft's Raymond Chen. The anti-piracy holograms were a way of assuring the buyer of a copy of Windows 95 that the product was legitimate. They're incredibly hard to fake, or just cost too much to produce, so even if one could successfully mimic the look of a Windows 95 box, they couldn't mimic the hologram.

The original hologram design had a baby sitting, which, when you moved the box, would show the child pointing and looking at the PC. In it, the baby had no top on.

Harking back to a separate blog post they wrote back in 2003, Chen claims a government (which "shall remain nameless for obvious reasons") saw that baby with no top, and while the hologram cuts off below the waist, assumed it to be entirely naked anyway. Microsoft then had to swiftly put out a second box with a fresh anti-piracy hologram, this time giving the baby a shirt and overalls.

As this was rushed to production, the second fully clothed hologram did not point at the Microsoft logo on the monitor. If you're wondering why Chen wrote this blog post now, over 20 years later, it's because a user posted a YouTube short of the original half-clothed baby hologram, which has seemingly become quite rare.

In 2003, Chen lamented that Windows "brings out the Rorschach test in everyone" and said: "If the baby in your hologram isn’t wearing a shirt, you have a genuine collector’s item."

I'm not too sure I want a collector's item purely because one world government thought it depicted a naked baby, but it certainly does seem pretty rare, and it's got to be one of the strangest anti-piracy holograms out there.

Given Windows 95 came out in, you guessed it, 1995, and the baby was likely a few years old at the time of making the hologram, one can assume the baby is now in at least their mid 30s. Here's hoping for Windows 12; we get a recreation of the Hologram with the now 30-something-year-old, but please keep the overalls this time.

articles.title: The Utility App Flood Won’t Last
articles.subtitle: The App Store is evolving at a breakneck pace not seen since its earliest days. We saw the first glimmers of what was to come early in 2025, but it wasn’t until late last year that the tsunami of apps developed with the help of AI agents really took hold.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
The App Store is evolving at a breakneck pace not seen since its earliest days. We saw the first glimmers of what was to come early in 2025, but it wasn’t until late last year that the tsunami of apps developed with the help of AI agents really took hold.

Since then, veteran developers are releasing new apps and updating existing ones faster than ever, and new developers are releasing their first apps in droves. Today, supply is dramatically up, demand is flat, and quality is seemingly simultaneously up and down, depending on where you look.

How these forces play out long-term is anyone’s guess, but it’s worth examining because, just as Federico’s link to Bryan Irace’s post about agentic coding tools foreshadowed the rise of tools like Codex and Claude Code, today’s trends are sparks that have the potential to become tomorrow’s App Store wildfires or simply fizzle out.

Utility apps are on the front lines of this change. The TechCrunch story I linked in April picked up on this trend:

Another interesting tidbit from Appfigures is that the Utilities app category moved up the top five chart.

If anything, the trend has accelerated in the months since.

It’s not surprising at all that utility apps have taken off. They’ve been a staple of new developers since long before agents came along. That’s because many are UI wrappers around command line tools. That isn’t a knock against the developers of those apps; most users don’t want to open Terminal to convert a video or audio file to another format using ffmpeg, for example. By building a great UI around command line tools, developers have made them far easier to use.

However, the relative simplicity and narrow scope of many utility apps have made them a natural fit for AI agents, too. That’s why the App Store (and my inbox) is deluged with Mac menu bar and single-screen iPhone and iPad utility apps.

On the one hand, the abundance of utilities has been great for users. More choice means you’re more likely to find the app that perfectly fits your needs.

On the other hand, though, I don’t think what’s happening in the category is sustainable and expect to see it dramatically shift again in the coming months. As we’ve seen from reporting by The New York Times, app supply is outstripping demand by orders of magnitude, which will drive down prices. That alone is likely to cause the utility app market to shrink. But there’s more to it than that.

Remember, the demand shifts that The New York Times reported, based on Sensor Tower numbers, are for the entire App Store, where download numbers have grown 2-3% this year and last. I expect utility downloads to actually shrink in the coming months – again, because of agents.

Utilities, especially simple ones, are exactly the sorts of apps that are becoming trivially easy for power users – the very users these utilities are made for – to create themselves. From frontier labs‘ model improvements to a growing number of app-building tools from those same labs and third parties, it’s never been easier to build a web or native app yourself.

And although I agree with people, like Nilay Patel, who say the notion that everyone will build their own software is overblown, the utility market is different. Your average person is not downloading apps to adjust the frame rate and file format of a video or downloading YouTube videos to watch later.

But those are exactly the sort of things that people who are using agents are doing with them, whether they’re having an agent do those things directly via a command line tool in an app like Codex or Claude Code or building an app to do the same thing. That’s going to put even more pressure on the category.

That said, I think there will always be a cohort of users who would rather pay for an app than build it themselves, so I’m not predicting the demise of utilities in general – just the end of today’s frothy market. I also think there remains a place for simple utilities that solve hard problems with clever solutions. Not every utility is a UI wrapper for a terminal command. Plenty of apps feature original solutions or thoughtful and unconventional remixes of disparate tools.

Utilities aren’t going away, but just like other App Store deluges, the trend will recede. It’s just that this time, it’s likely to flip faster than usual.

articles.title: New OLED ROG Xbox Ally X Almost Feels Like A Bargain In The Current RAMpocalypse
articles.subtitle: Asus OLED ROG Xbox Ally X I was somewhat cold on the Asus ROG Xbox Ally X when I reviewed it last fall, and for good reason.
articles.author: Kotaku
articles.content:
Asus OLED ROG Xbox Ally X

I was somewhat cold on the Asus ROG Xbox Ally X when I reviewed it last fall, and for good reason. The software layer was not good, and game performance on Windows comes with compromises that are hard to ignore for the $1,000 price tag. A year later, I feel much more sympathetic as RAMageddon spikes hardware prices across the gaming ecosystem. It’s in that context that Asus has chosen to reveal the price of its new Xbox Ally X20 that comes with an OLED screen: $1,300.

A year ago, my eyeballs would have jumped out of their sockets like a Looney Tunes character at a $1,300 price tag. But after a year of using the ROG Ally X, watching the price of every other option balloon, and desperately wishing the Switch 2 had an OLED option, it actually feels like a reasonable upgrade, all things considered. In addition to the OLED display, the Xbox Ally X20 has TMR joysticks and a new D-pad.

It’s translucent black with some gold flourishes on the shell. Otherwise, it’s the same specs inside the machine.

OLED options are few and far between in the PC gaming handheld market. The closest competitor to the new Xbox Ally X20 is the Lenovo Legion Go 2, which also has an OLED screen, comes with detachable controllers, and has more RAM. That device is $1,350. There’s also the Steam Deck OLED, which used to be $650 and is now $950. It offers a much more seamless, console-like experience but has significantly lower specs than the Ally X.

Depending on what you want out of a PC gaming handheld, the Xbox Ally X20 still might lose out to these other devices in various categories, but the margins are getting much thinner as everything gets more expensive. Suddenly, the premium version of a premium handheld doesn’t feel so overpriced. The real selling point of the Ally X is still being able to combine the benefits of Game Pass with the breadth of Steam, so for those uninterested in the Xbox ecosystem, it’s a nonstarter.

But if Microsoft can actually deliver a streamlined, performance-improving version of Windows for gaming at some point, the Xbox Ally X20 could have a claim to being the best PC gaming handheld around.

There’s big news in the land of small desktops. Jason Snell at Six Colors:

In a bit of a late-August surprise while the world awaits word on the next generation of iPhones, on Tuesday Apple announced two new processors, the M5 Ultra and M6, which help power new iterations of its Mac Studio and Mac mini desktop computers.

Mac mini with M6 and M5 Pro

The M6 is built with a new 2-nanometer process and comes with 12 CPU cores, up from the 10 found in the base M4 and M5. It packs six efficiency cores, four performance cores, and two super cores. Snell explains:

According to Apple, each core design is focused on a different primary task: efficiency cores are meant to sip power (useful when running simple background tasks); performance cores are optimized for complex, multi-threaded jobs; and super cores were created to offer the highest possible single-threaded performance.

The higher-end Mac mini is now powered by the M5 Pro. Both Mac mini models include Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, 2.5Gb Ethernet (10Gb is an option), and both top out at 64 GB of unified memory. If you need 8 TB of storage, the M5 Pro is required.

Mac Studio with M5 Max & M5 Ultra

Since March of last year, the Mac Studio has been available with either an M4 Max or an M3 Ultra SoC, with RAM upgrade options dwindling over time.

No more! Now users can choose between the M5 Max previously seen in the MacBook Pro, or an all-new M5 Ultra. The former is available with an 18-core CPU and 32-core GPU or an 18-core CPU and 40-core GPU. The Ultra also comes in two variants: one with a 30-core CPU and 64-core GPU, and one with 36 CPU cores paired to 80 GPU cores. RAM tops out at 256 GB for the Max, with a 512 GB option coming in October for the Ultra.

You can get 16 TB of storage for a cool $7,500, but it requires the M5 Ultra.

Pricing & Avaibility

Because we’re in 2026, these new machines come with new starting prices:

M6 Mac mini: $899 (+$100)

M5 Pro Mac mini: $1,699 (+$100)

M5 Max Mac Studio: $2,499 (unchanged)

M5 Ultra Mac Studio: $5,499 (+$200)

These new prices are on top of Apple’s recently announced price increases. For comparison, the M4 Mac mini started at $499, while the M4 Max Mac Studio was initially sold for $1,999.

The new Mac mini and Mac Studio ship on September 22 and will both require macOS Golden Gate.

Liquid AI’s Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs) will be adapted for Mac-based assistance and combined with MacPaw’s own on-device technologies: Mnemos for memory and Elix for inference.

Eney already shifted to a local model last year, keeping reasoning, contextual search, skill execution, and conversation history on the device whenever possible.

The new partnership is intended to push that approach further. The two companies are jointly developing the underlying stack rather than MacPaw simply adding another third-party model.

Once the technology has been tested and implemented in Eney, MacPaw says it plans to bring it to more of its products. It also wants to make the shared AI stack available to Mac developers through Setapp.

That could let participating apps expose more of their capabilities and context to Eney. This would allow the assistant to understand what is inside an app. It could also provide more useful answers or take relevant actions.

You can learn more about MacPaw’s on-device AI technology and today’s announcement here, and catch up on Liquid AI here.

articles.title: Apple’s AI announcements: One big question, and 11 key features
articles.subtitle: Almost two years after Apple first showed off a video promoting the new Siri and lots of exciting new Apple Intelligence features, that future has finally arrived – at least in first beta form. The company had a lot of ground to make up.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Almost two years after Apple first showed off a video promoting the new Siri and lots of exciting new Apple Intelligence features, that future has finally arrived – at least in first beta form.

The company had a lot of ground to make up. Obviously, the test will be how well the new features work in real life usage, but let’s start with what seemed to me to be the most important things the company announced …

The big iPhone support question

For me, one of the biggest questions to arise from the keynote was exactly what features will require the iPhone 17 Pro and up?

Apple had three things to say about iPhone support. The first says that any phone capable of running iOS 26 can be upgraded to iOS 27. That means all the way back to the iPhone 11.

The second is that the new AI features only extend back to the iPhone 15 Pro:

Apple Intelligence and Siri AI in iOS 27, iPadOS 27, macOS 27, watchOS 27, and visionOS 27 are available on iPhone 16 models or later, iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max.

The third says that some features are limited to just the latest and greatest models.

Apple’s most powerful on-device model and the features it enables, like expressive voices and more advanced dictation, are available on iPhone Air, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro Max.

The word ‘like’ is doing a lot of heavy lifting there: it means we don’t yet know what other features will fall into this category. Additionally, it’s not yet 100% clear whether phones that can’t perform these actions on-device will still get access to the same features, just relying on cloud connectivity.

This latter question is especially important when it comes to advanced dictation. However smart the new Siri may be, it first needs to understand what we are saying. The existing Siri speech-to-text capabilities fall way short of what is available from third-parties.

The overall model seems well-considered

Apple’s general approach here is to make Siri’s new capabilities transparently available system-wide. In other words, we can ask our iPhone to do something and the new Siri will step in to perform the task.

However, there are times when it’s useful to revisit an earlier chatbot session, and Apple allows us to do this through the Siri app. That seems to me the best of both worlds. We don’t need to open Siri to do anything requiring the new Apple Intelligence features, but we can access past sessions when required.

Agentic AI is key

The ability to ask our iPhone to carry out a task and have it be able to access not only the personal information we have stored on our phone, but also interact with apps, is absolutely key to truly useful AI.

Again, we will need to see how well this really works, but Apple does seem to be ticking all of the boxes in terms of the capabilities I was looking for.

articles.title: Hideo Kojima wants to 'continue to focus on making games' at 63, even as 'the time I have decreases'
articles.subtitle: "I need to constantly scrutinize how I use my time and how I live my life."
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
It's often said that time comes for us all—and while it may not yet be at the doorstep of one Hideo Kojima, he's grown introspective about the prospect on social media after turning 63 over the weekend. In case you've somehow not heard of the man, he's the mind behind the Metal Gear series and Death Stranding.

"I've turned 63," Kojima posted to X. "As I get older, the things I 'have to do' and the things I 'want to do' keep increasing. On the other hand, the 'time I have' decreases. I need to constantly scrutinize how I use my time and how I live my life."

It's a particularly nostalgic date for Kojima, however, as 2026 also "marks the 40th anniversary of when I started making games, and the 10th anniversary of Kojima Productions." To celebrate, he intends to hold an exhibition at Tokyo's Azabudai Hills Gallery starting at the end of October and lasting until the end of the year.

To those fearing his flooded schedule and nostalgic thoughts might precede a retirement from games, though, rest easy. Kojima's flooded schedule is more of a motivator than a detractor: "With all the opportunities and offers I'm receiving, I want to continue to focus on making games. Thank you for your continued support."

Which, hey, is a relief even as someone not particularly attached to either of his flagship franchises—not for purposes of taste, mind. With an industry where big-budget games are coming out with increasingly bland, characterless stories, I'm charmed pink whenever I see some out-of-context Death Stranding cutscene where Tommie Earl Jenkins breaks out into song, or Troy Baker plays guitar while dressed up like a cyberpunk Joker.

It's hard to imagine an industry without Kojima, though it'll happen someday. At which point he'll apparently be watching movie trailers.
